subject: English
description: Subject-verb agreement: collective nouns, indefinite pronouns, correlative conjunctions, fractions, special nouns

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The team ___ playing exceptionally well this season.'
questions.explanation: 'Team' is a collective noun treated as a singular unit in formal Indian/exam English. It takes a singular verb 'is'. In British informal usage 'are' can appear, but in competitive exams the default is singular for collective nouns acting as a unit.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Neither of the students ___ answered the question correctly.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb. 'Neither' is an indefinite pronoun that refers to not one of two, and it is always singular: 'Neither of the students IS'. Compare: 'Neither student is' — same rule.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The dogs in the yard ___ barking loudly.'
questions.explanation: The subject is 'dogs' (plural), not 'yard'. The prepositional phrase 'in the yard' is a modifier and does not affect verb agreement. Plural subject 'dogs' takes plural verb 'are'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Everyone ___ present at the annual general meeting.'
questions.explanation: Indefinite pronouns ending in '-one', '-body', '-thing' (everyone, somebody, anything, etc.) always take singular verbs. 'Everyone WAS present' — this rule has no exceptions in standard grammar.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The news from the flood-affected areas ___ deeply shocking.'
questions.explanation: 'News' appears plural due to the '-s' ending but is an uncountable singular noun. It always takes a singular verb: 'The news IS'. Other similar nouns: information, advice, furniture, equipment, luggage.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Physics ___ always been my most challenging subject.'
questions.explanation: Academic disciplines ending in '-ics' (physics, mathematics, economics, politics, ethics, athletics) are singular and take singular verbs: 'Physics HAS always been'. Do not confuse the '-s' ending with plurality.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Either she or they ___ responsible for the delay.'
questions.explanation: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it (proximity rule). 'They' (plural) is the nearer subject, so the verb is 'are'. If the order were reversed ('Either they or she'), the verb would be 'is'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'A bouquet of roses ___ placed on the podium.'
questions.explanation: The subject is 'bouquet' (singular), not 'roses'. The prepositional phrase 'of roses' modifies the head noun 'bouquet'. The verb agrees with the head noun: 'A bouquet WAS placed'. Don't be misled by 'roses' immediately before the verb.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The committee ___ announced its decision regarding the new policy.'
questions.explanation: 'Committee' is a collective noun acting as a single body (one decision, one 'its'). The pronoun 'its' (singular) confirms the committee is treated as a unit → singular verb 'has'. If the members act individually, 'are/have' might appear informally.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Neither the doctor nor the nurses ___ available at that hour.'
questions.explanation: Proximity rule: with 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearest subject. 'Nurses' (plural) is closest → 'were'. If the sentence read 'Neither the nurses nor the doctor', the verb would be 'was' (agreeing with 'doctor').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Forty percent of the students ___ already submitted their assignments.'
questions.explanation: With percentages and fractions, the verb agrees with the noun that follows 'of'. 'Students' is plural → 'have'. Compare: 'Forty percent of the report HAS been submitted' (report = singular).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Two and two ___ four.' (mathematical statement)
questions.explanation: In mathematical or proverbial statements, a compound subject formed by 'and' can take a singular verb when the two items form an inseparable single idea or result: 'Two and two MAKES four'. This is an exception to the normal 'X and Y = plural' rule.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The books on the top shelf ___ covered in dust.'
questions.explanation: The subject is 'books' (plural). 'On the top shelf' is a prepositional phrase modifier. Strip it away: 'The books ___ covered in dust' → plural subject → 'are'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Swimming in the river ___ good exercise for the whole body.'
questions.explanation: A gerund (verb + -ing) used as the subject of a sentence is always singular: 'Swimming IS'. Other examples: 'Running every day is healthy', 'Reading books improves vocabulary'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The list of required documents ___ on the official website.'
questions.explanation: Head noun = 'list' (singular). 'Of required documents' is a prepositional modifier. 'List IS'. Compare: 'The documents ARE on the website' — same documents, but now 'documents' is the head noun.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The number of road accidents in the city ___ decreased significantly.'
questions.explanation: 'The number of' = singular (the number itself is one quantity). Compare: 'A number of' = plural (= several). Key rule: 'The number HAS' but 'A number HAVE'. This distinction is heavily tested.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'A number of candidates ___ absent on the day of the examination.'
questions.explanation: 'A number of' = 'several/many' and takes a plural verb. 'A number of candidates WERE absent'. Contrast with 'The number of candidates WAS larger than expected' (the number itself, singular).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Half of the annual report ___ already been submitted to the board.'
questions.explanation: Fraction + 'of' → verb agrees with the noun following 'of'. 'Report' is singular → 'has'. Compare the next question where 'reports' (plural) changes the verb.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Half of the quarterly reports ___ already been reviewed.'
questions.explanation: 'Reports' is plural → 'have'. The fraction 'half of' doesn't determine the verb — the noun after 'of' does. 'Half of the reports HAVE been reviewed' vs 'Half of the report HAS been reviewed'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The jury ___ delivered a unanimous verdict after three days.'
questions.explanation: 'Jury' is a collective noun acting as a single unit (one unanimous verdict). Singular verb 'has'. The pronoun 'a unanimous verdict' further confirms unity. If jurors acted individually, 'have' might appear informally.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'The team of experts have submitted their detailed report to the government.'
questions.explanation: The head noun is 'team' (singular collective noun acting as a unit), not 'experts'. The verb must be 'has submitted its' (both verb and pronoun need to be singular). Correct: 'The team of experts has submitted its report...'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Each of the boys ___ received a prize at the annual function.'
questions.explanation: 'Each of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb. 'Each' is an indefinite pronoun that always refers to individuals one by one — it is inherently singular. 'Each of the boys HAS received'. Similarly, 'every', 'each', 'either', 'neither' are all singular.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: '___ there any important messages left for me while I was away?'
questions.explanation: In 'There + verb + subject' structures, the verb agrees with the real subject (what comes after the verb). 'Messages' is plural → 'Were there'. The subject is delayed but the agreement still applies to it.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The poor ___ always in need of support from society.'
questions.explanation: 'The + adjective' used as a collective noun (the poor, the rich, the elderly, the sick, the brave) is always plural: 'The poor ARE'. These refer to entire classes of people.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Many a brave soldier have sacrificed their lives for the nation.'
questions.explanation: 'Many a + singular noun' always takes a singular verb: 'Many a soldier HAS', not 'have'. Despite 'many' suggesting plurality, 'many a' grammatically functions like 'each/every' + singular noun. Correct: 'Many a brave soldier has sacrificed his life'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Tom and Jerry ___ a popular cartoon series that has entertained generations.'
questions.explanation: Titles of books, films, shows, or artistic works take singular verbs even if the title contains plural-sounding words: 'Tom and Jerry IS a cartoon series'. The title names one entity.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The quality of the mangoes available in this market ___ very poor.'
questions.explanation: Head noun = 'quality' (singular). 'Of the mangoes available in this market' is a long modifier. Strip it: 'The quality IS very poor'. Long intervening phrases often mislead — always identify the true subject.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Three-fourths of the wall ___ already been painted by the workers.'
questions.explanation: Fraction + 'of' → verb agrees with noun after 'of'. 'Wall' is singular → 'has been painted'. Compare next question where 'students' (plural) changes the answer.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Three-fourths of the students ___ already passed the preliminary screening.'
questions.explanation: 'Students' is plural → 'have'. Fraction rule: always look at the noun after 'of'. The fraction (1/2, 3/4, etc.) itself is irrelevant to verb agreement.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'The scissors is kept in the top drawer of my desk.'
questions.explanation: 'Scissors' is a plural-only noun (always ends in '-s', refers to two blades). It requires a plural verb: 'The scissors ARE kept'. Other plural-only nouns: trousers, glasses, pliers, tongs, tweezers.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'No news ___ good news — that is the old saying.'
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable singular noun (not a plural of 'new'). It always takes a singular verb. This sentence is also a proverb/fixed expression where the singular verb is invariable.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The rich and the powerful ___ sometimes indifferent to the struggles of common people.'
questions.explanation: 'The rich' and 'the powerful' each refer to groups of people (plural). Two such groups joined by 'and' form a plural compound subject → 'are'. Both expressions individually are plural: 'The rich ARE...' and 'The powerful ARE...'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Either the players or the coach ___ to blame for the poor performance.'
questions.explanation: Proximity rule for 'either...or': verb agrees with the nearest subject. 'Coach' (singular) is nearest → 'is'. If the order were 'Either the coach or the players', the verb would be 'are' (players is nearest).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Bread and butter ___ the only food available at the refugee camp.'
questions.explanation: When two things are customarily thought of as one combined item (bread and butter, rice and curry, rod and line), a singular verb is used. 'Bread and butter IS a comfort food'. This is a notional agreement exception.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'More than one student were absent during the surprise inspection.'
questions.explanation: 'More than one + singular noun' takes a singular verb: 'More than one student WAS absent'. Despite the logical meaning implying plurality, the grammatical rule is clear: 'more than one' treats the noun as singular. Correct: 'More than one student was absent.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The mathematics of the problem ___ extremely complex and confusing.'
questions.explanation: 'Mathematics' as a discipline is singular. However, even when referring to 'the mathematics of [something]' (i.e., the calculations involved), the verb remains singular: 'The mathematics IS'. Don't confuse with 'mathematical steps' (which would be plural).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Neither of them ___ willing to compromise on the deadline.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither of them' — 'neither' is singular. Even though 'them' (plural) follows, 'neither' governs agreement. 'Neither of them IS willing'. This is one of the most frequently tested indefinite pronoun rules.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The police ___ been deployed across all sensitive areas of the city.'
questions.explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun (it refers to a body of individual officers, no singular 'a police'). It always takes a plural verb: 'The police HAVE been deployed'. Similarly: 'cattle', 'clergy', 'people', 'gentry' are all plural without a singular form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Slow and steady ___ the race — this proverb has guided many.'
questions.explanation: In proverbs and fixed expressions, 'slow and steady' is treated as a single subject (a single concept/approach) → singular verb 'wins'. This is similar to 'bread and butter IS' — two words functioning as one idea.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Politics ___ never been a clean game, according to historians.'
questions.explanation: 'Politics' (like 'economics', 'mathematics', 'ethics') ends in '-ics' but functions as a singular noun when referring to the field as a whole: 'Politics HAS never been clean'. When referring to specific activities, it can sometimes be plural, but in competitive exams, the singular form is standard.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'A number of people has already registered for the annual marathon.'
questions.explanation: 'A number of' = 'several/many' → plural verb: 'have already registered'. The error is using singular 'has'. Remember the key contrast: 'A number of people HAVE registered' vs 'The number of registrations HAS increased'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Neither courage nor the skills required ___ sufficient to overcome destiny.'
questions.explanation: Proximity rule: 'neither...nor' → verb agrees with nearest subject. 'The skills required' (plural) is nearest → 'are'. If the order were 'neither the skills nor courage', the verb would be 'is' (courage is singular and nearest).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'The audience were requested to remain seated until the ceremony ended.'
questions.explanation: 'Audience' is a collective noun treated as a single unit in formal/exam English → singular verb: 'was requested'. In informal British usage, collective nouns can take plural verbs (members acting individually), but Indian competitive exams expect the singular form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'One of the factors that ___ crucial to success is consistent practice.'
questions.explanation: In 'one of the [plural noun] that/who...', the relative pronoun 'that' refers to the plural noun ('factors'), so the verb in the relative clause is plural: 'factors that ARE crucial'. The main clause verb ('is') agrees with 'one'. Two separate agreements in one sentence.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'Mathematics, along with physics and chemistry, ___ compulsory in the first semester.'
questions.explanation: Phrases like 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', 'in addition to' do NOT create compound subjects. The verb agrees only with the first (main) subject. Subject = 'Mathematics' (singular) → 'is'. The parenthetical phrase 'along with physics and chemistry' is additional information.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The team, including its captain and vice-captain, ___ ready for the crucial final.'
questions.explanation: 'Including its captain and vice-captain' is a parenthetical phrase that does not alter the subject. Subject = 'team' (singular collective noun) → 'is'. The pronoun 'its' further confirms singular treatment.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'Every man and every woman have a unique role to play in nation-building.'
questions.explanation: 'Every + noun + and + every + noun' takes a singular verb. 'Every' distributes the meaning individually, not collectively. Correct: 'Every man and every woman HAS a unique role'. Similarly: 'Each boy and each girl was present'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'The number of applications received this year ___ grown by over 40 percent.'
questions.explanation: 'The number of' → singular → 'has grown'. Recap: 'The number of [things]' = one number (singular); 'A number of [things]' = many things (plural). This contrast is one of the highest-frequency SVA questions in SSC CGL and IBPS exams.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: 'What ___ needed most is sustained effort and consistent revision.'
questions.explanation: 'What' used as a subject is treated as singular when it introduces a singular idea (= 'the thing that'). 'What is needed IS sustained effort.' The complement 'effort and revision' is plural, but the grammatical subject 'what' controls the verb and takes singular agreement.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error: 'The cattle in the northern pasture grazes near the river every morning.'

options.option_text: The cattle in the northern pasture

questions.explanation: 'Cattle' is an inherently plural noun (like 'police', 'people'). There is no singular 'a cattle'. Plural verb required: 'The cattle GRAZE near the river'. 'Grazes' is the third-person singular form, which is incorrect here.
questions.subject: English
